coverage.learning_objective: Select an operator AWS CLI profile

required_facts.statement: A named AWS CLI profile groups credential and configuration settings; select it with --profile NAME.
Run aws sts get-caller-identity --profile NAME to inspect the caller ARN and account ID.
Run aws configure list --profile NAME to inspect the effective configuration and where its values came from; --region REGION overrides the configured Region for a command.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: You are about to operate in a sandbox, but your workstation has more than one approved AWS context. Before issuing a resource-changing command, make the chosen context explicit. A profile name is a starting point for checking the caller, not a substitute for checking it.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A named AWS CLI profile groups credential and configuration settings; select it with --profile NAME.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Run aws sts get-caller-identity --profile NAME to inspect the caller ARN and account ID.

Run aws configure list --profile NAME to inspect the effective configuration and where its values came from; --region REGION overrides the configured Region for a command.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the exercise supplies a profile named lab-operator and expects a particular account. Run aws sts get-caller-identity --profile lab-operator. Suppose the illustrative result shows Account: [REDACTED_ACCOUNT] and Arn: arn:aws:iam::[REDACTED_ACCOUNT]:user/[REDACTED_OPERATOR]. Compare both values with the supplied operator context: this checks the caller identity and account. Then run aws configure list --profile lab-operator. Suppose its illustrative Region row shows Value: us-west-2, Type: config-file, Location: ~/.aws/config. This checks the effective Region and its configuration origin rather than inferring them from the profile's label. If the approved command targets a different Region, substitute that Region for REGION in its --region option. Keep the same explicit profile on the command. This example checks identity and effective configuration separately: knowing which account is selected does not answer which Region the command will use.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Do not treat an account check as a Region check. get-caller-identity inspects the caller ARN and account ID; configure list inspects effective configuration and its origins. --region overrides the configured Region for that command, not the meaning of the caller ARN.

video_need.reason: Comparing caller identity, effective configuration origins and an explicit Region override benefits from a short terminal demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Select the supplied approved lab-operator context and confirm its caller identity, account and effective Region before proceeding with a supplied sandbox command.
practice_anchor.success: Use aws sts get-caller-identity --profile lab-operator and compare the returned ARN and account ID with the supplied expected context. Use aws configure list --profile lab-operator to identify the effective Region and its source. Keep --profile lab-operator on the supplied sandbox command and, when its approved target Region differs from the configured Region, select that target with --region REGION. Complete these checks before proceeding, without creating or changing credentials.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the lab-operator profile selection, caller ARN and account ID, and configure list Region value, Type and Location visible in a simulated terminal. Distinguish the configured Region from an explicit --region option on the supplied sandbox command.

teaching_notes: Keep credential creation out of scope; use supplied approved operator credentials and require the external secrets-handling preparation.

context.concept_name: Allocate VPC and subnet CIDRs after external IP-addressing/CIDR preparation

coverage.learning_objective: Allocate nonoverlapping VPC and subnet CIDRs

required_facts.statement: An IPv4 subnet CIDR must be within its VPC CIDR and must not overlap another subnet in that VPC.
IPv4 subnet sizes range from /16 to /28; AWS reserves the first four addresses and the last address of each subnet.
Choose subnet ranges inside the VPC that do not intersect, and allow for the five reserved addresses when checking usable capacity.
Each subnet resides entirely in one Availability Zone; create separate subnets for workloads in different Availability Zones.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A lab needs two subnets for workloads placed in different Availability Zones. Address allocation has two separate questions: do the ranges fit without overlap, and does each range leave enough usable addresses? Complete the external IP-addressing and CIDR preparation before this AWS-specific allocation.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An IPv4 subnet CIDR must be within its VPC CIDR and must not overlap another subnet in that VPC.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
IPv4 subnet sizes range from /16 to /28; AWS reserves the first four addresses and the last address of each subnet.

Choose subnet ranges inside the VPC that do not intersect, and allow for the five reserved addresses when checking usable capacity.

Each subnet resides entirely in one Availability Zone; create separate subnets for workloads in different Availability Zones.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Take a supplied VPC range of 10.20.0.0/16. Two candidate subnets are 10.20.1.0/24 and 10.20.2.0/24. They lie inside that VPC and do not intersect. A /24 contains 256 addresses; after the five AWS reservations, 251 remain usable. For 10.20.1.0/24, the reserved addresses are .0 through .3 and .255. Compare 251 with the supplied capacity requirement, not 256. Place the two separate subnets in the two intended Availability Zones. Now consider changing the second candidate to 10.20.1.128/25: that range lies inside the first subnet, so it fails the nonoverlap check even though it is inside the VPC. Containment and nonoverlap are distinct tests, and both must pass.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A larger VPC does not make overlapping subnet ranges valid. Nor does an address count before reservations establish usable capacity. Check the VPC boundary, intersections with other subnets, and usable addresses separately; a subnet also belongs wholly to one Availability Zone.

video_need.reason: Nested and overlapping CIDR ranges plus reserved subnet addresses are easier to compare in an address-range diagram.

practice_anchor.objective: Allocate two subnet CIDRs within the supplied VPC 10.20.0.0/16, assigning one subnet to each of two supplied Availability Zones. Select from candidate ranges to provide at least 200 usable IPv4 addresses per subnet.
practice_anchor.success: Both selected subnet CIDRs are within 10.20.0.0/16, do not overlap, and have prefix lengths within /16 through /28. Each provides at least 200 usable addresses after subtracting the five AWS-reserved addresses, and each is assigned entirely to a different supplied Availability Zone.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show 10.20.1.0/24 and 10.20.2.0/24 as nonintersecting ranges inside VPC 10.20.0.0/16, with one subnet assigned to each Availability Zone. Contrast the overlapping candidate 10.20.1.128/25 inside 10.20.1.0/24. Annotate the first four and last reserved addresses of each /24 and its 251 usable addresses.

teaching_notes: Do not reteach CIDR arithmetic; require demonstrated external networking.ip_addressing_and_cidr mastery.

context.concept_name: Compare ECS and managed EKS operational ownership

coverage.learning_objective: Choose ECS or managed EKS from an operational-ownership requirement

required_facts.statement: ECS is a managed container orchestration service that schedules container workloads; customers supply and operate their applications.
Managed EKS runs the Kubernetes control plane; customers retain responsibility for workload configuration and, depending on the compute option, worker nodes.
Choose between ECS and EKS by comparing the need for Kubernetes APIs and ecosystem with the team’s willingness to operate Kubernetes workloads.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A team choosing a container platform asks who will operate each part of it. The useful comparison is not simply whether a service is managed. Identify which platform work the service handles and which workload work remains with the team.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: ECS is a managed container orchestration service that schedules container workloads; customers supply and operate their applications.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Managed EKS runs the Kubernetes control plane; customers retain responsibility for workload configuration and, depending on the compute option, worker nodes.

Choose between ECS and EKS by comparing the need for Kubernetes APIs and ecosystem with the team’s willingness to operate Kubernetes workloads.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Imagine an approved workload requirement that calls for Kubernetes APIs and its ecosystem. Managed EKS supplies the Kubernetes control plane, but the team still configures and operates Kubernetes workloads; worker-node responsibility depends on the selected compute option. Compare that requirement with an alternative that only needs managed container scheduling and can be operated through ECS. Record both the platform requirement and the remaining customer duties. The choice should reflect the team's willingness to operate those workloads, not just a preference for the word managed. This is an ownership comparison, not an exercise in administering a self-managed Kubernetes control plane.

For a second requirement, suppose the supplied application has no Kubernetes API dependency. That removes the stated platform reason for selecting EKS, but it does not remove the need to operate the application on ECS. Describe the remaining workload duty under both proposals. A comparison that says AWS manages everything for either service would hide the very ownership boundary the decision is meant to evaluate.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Managed does not mean the application is operated for you. ECS customers supply and operate applications; EKS customers retain workload configuration responsibilities and may retain worker-node duties. Keep that compute-option qualification when describing EKS ownership.

video_need.reason: The service comparison is an ownership classification; a compact responsibility table is enough and no tool demonstration is needed.

practice_anchor.objective: Select ECS or managed EKS for a supplied team's Kubernetes API and ecosystem requirements and willingness to operate Kubernetes workloads. Select the corresponding platform and customer responsibilities, preserving the compute-option qualification for EKS worker nodes.
practice_anchor.success: The selected platform fits the supplied requirements and operating constraints. The responsibility selections identify ECS-managed container scheduling and customer-operated applications, or the EKS-managed Kubernetes control plane and customer workload configuration, with worker-node responsibility dependent on the compute option.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the ownership comparison visible in a compact ECS-versus-managed-EKS table showing managed platform duties, retained customer workload duties, the compute-dependent EKS worker-node qualification, and the Kubernetes requirements and team willingness that guide the choice.

teaching_notes: Keep this comparison short; do not introduce self-managed Kubernetes administration.

context.concept_name: Configure subnet internet routing, teaching route-table association and CIDR destination routes; assume only external CIDR/IP addressing

required_facts.statement: A subnet uses its explicitly associated route table or, without an explicit association, the VPC main route table.
Among matching destination routes, the most specific destination prefix takes priority.
Associate the subnet with the intended route table and add an IPv4 0.0.0.0/0 route targeting the attached internet gateway for internet-bound destinations not matched by a more specific route.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A subnet's intended internet route has been added to a route table, yet the operator still needs to establish which table the subnet actually uses. Routing starts with association, then destination matching. Use the CIDR knowledge completed in external preparation.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: A subnet uses its explicitly associated route table or, without an explicit association, the VPC main route table.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Among matching destination routes, the most specific destination prefix takes priority.

Associate the subnet with the intended route table and add an IPv4 0.0.0.0/0 route targeting the attached internet gateway for internet-bound destinations not matched by a more specific route.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the intended table contains a route for 10.20.0.0/16 and an internet-gateway route for 0.0.0.0/0. A destination of 10.20.2.10 matches both prefixes; the /16 is more specific, so the default route does not take priority. An example destination of 198.51.100.8 matches the default route when no more specific destination route applies. Before reasoning from those entries, inspect the subnet's association. If it has no explicit association, it uses the VPC main table, which may not be the table you edited. Associate the subnet with the intended table and check the default route's target is the attached internet gateway. The routing claim here is about the selected route, not a claim that every other requirement for a working connection has been met.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Adding 0.0.0.0/0 is not an instruction to override every other route. More specific matching destinations take priority. Also, editing a table is not proof that a subnet uses it: an explicit association or the main-table fallback determines that.

video_need.reason: A subnet association diagram and competing destination prefixes clarify main-table fallback and longest-prefix route selection.

practice_anchor.objective: Associate the supplied subnet with the intended route table and configure an IPv4 0.0.0.0/0 route targeting the supplied internet gateway, which is already attached to the VPC.
practice_anchor.success: The subnet is explicitly associated with the intended route table. That table retains its 10.20.0.0/16 route and contains a 0.0.0.0/0 route targeting the supplied attached internet gateway.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show a subnet using the VPC main route table before explicit association and the intended table afterward. Display that table's 10.20.0.0/16 and 0.0.0.0/0 routes, highlighting the /16 match for 10.20.2.10 and the internet-gateway default route for 198.51.100.8 when no more specific route matches.

teaching_notes: Teach route selection only; leave security rules and end-to-end connectivity diagnosis to their later concepts.

context.concept_name: Define recovery time and recovery point objectives

coverage.learning_objective: Set recovery time and recovery point objectives

required_facts.statement: Recovery time objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable time to restore service after a disruption.
Recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.
Set recovery objectives from business requirements and use them to choose recovery capabilities that meet the tolerated downtime and data loss.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A business owner says a service may be unavailable briefly, but only a small amount of recent data may be lost. Those are two requirements, not one general promise of fast recovery. Name the tolerated downtime and tolerated data loss separately.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Recovery time objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable time to restore service after a disruption.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.

Set recovery objectives from business requirements and use them to choose recovery capabilities that meet the tolerated downtime and data loss.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: For an illustrative requirement, suppose the owner accepts at most 30 minutes to restore service and at most 5 minutes of lost data. Record RTO as 30 minutes and RPO as 5 minutes. The first number answers how long service restoration may take after disruption; the second answers how much data loss, measured in time, is acceptable. A proposed recovery capability must be compared with both requirements. If its restoration time meets 30 minutes but its recoverable data is 20 minutes behind the disruption, it does not satisfy the stated data-loss objective. Conversely, sufficiently recent data does not by itself establish timely restoration. These numbers are example business requirements, not recommended AWS defaults.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: RPO is not another name for recovery duration. RTO bounds the time to restore service; RPO bounds acceptable data loss measured in time. Derive both from the business requirement rather than choosing whichever number is easiest to meet.

video_need.reason: RTO and RPO are two business-requirement definitions; a small timestamp comparison suffices without a tool demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: For one supplied workload, select RTO and RPO from the owner's stated downtime and data-loss tolerances. Choose a recovery approach from supplied options with stated restoration times and data-loss intervals, and justify the choice against both objectives.
practice_anchor.success: RTO matches the maximum tolerated service-restoration time, RPO matches the maximum tolerated data loss measured in time, and the selected approach meets both limits. The justification compares each supplied capability with its corresponding business requirement.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the example workload's 30-minute downtime tolerance and 5-minute data-loss tolerance beside candidate recovery approaches' restoration times and data-loss intervals, making visible that meeting only one limit is insufficient.

teaching_notes: Keep measurement and rehearsal procedures for the later recovery-verification concept.

context.concept_name: Distinguish AWS-managed and customer operational responsibilities

coverage.learning_objective: Assign AWS and customer operating responsibility

required_facts.statement: With EC2, customers manage the guest operating system, including updates and security patches.
With RDS, AWS manages database infrastructure and operating-system maintenance, while customers manage their data and application use.
Assign duties by the service boundary: AWS manages its infrastructure, while customers retain responsibilities for data, access and customer-controlled configuration.

Interpret the supplied EC2 OS-update report as customer guest-OS work and the supplied RDS parameter-check report as customer-controlled database configuration; RDS parameter groups contain database engine configuration values.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Two reports arrive in the operations queue: an EC2 operating-system update report and an RDS parameter-check report. To route the work correctly, look at what the service manages and what the customer still controls, rather than treating all managed services alike.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: With EC2, customers manage the guest operating system, including updates and security patches.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
With RDS, AWS manages database infrastructure and operating-system maintenance, while customers manage their data and application use.

Assign duties by the service boundary: AWS manages its infrastructure, while customers retain responsibilities for data, access and customer-controlled configuration.

Interpret the supplied EC2 OS-update report as customer guest-OS work and the supplied RDS parameter-check report as customer-controlled database configuration; RDS parameter groups contain database engine configuration values.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Label the EC2 report as customer guest-operating-system work, including updates and security patches. For the RDS report, distinguish AWS-managed database infrastructure and operating-system maintenance from the customer's data, application use and customer-controlled engine configuration. A parameter group contains database engine configuration values, so the supplied parameter-check report concerns customer-controlled configuration. In the handoff, name the service boundary alongside the report: guest OS for EC2, engine configuration values for this RDS check. That makes the assignment specific enough to act on without claiming the customer operates RDS infrastructure. Data and access responsibilities also remain part of the customer side of the boundary.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: AWS-managed infrastructure is not a blanket transfer of every operational duty. In particular, EC2 guest-OS patching remains customer work, while RDS operating-system maintenance is AWS work. RDS customer configuration and data duties still remain.

video_need.reason: EC2 and RDS responsibility boundaries can be communicated in a compact table without demonstrating platform operations.

practice_anchor.objective: Produce one responsibility assignment for a workload using EC2 and RDS by matching the supplied duties and reports to AWS or the customer and identifying the relevant service boundary.
practice_anchor.success: The assignment places EC2 guest-OS updates and security patches with the customer; RDS database infrastructure and operating-system maintenance with AWS; and data, access, application use and customer-controlled configuration with the customer. It classifies the EC2 OS-update report as customer guest-OS work and the RDS parameter-check report as customer-controlled database engine configuration.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the EC2 and RDS responsibility boundaries visible in a table of service, duty or supplied report, responsible party and boundary rationale. Distinguish EC2 guest-OS patching from RDS operating-system maintenance, and identify RDS parameter groups as database engine configuration values controlled by the customer.

teaching_notes: Do not introduce database capacity selection or specialist database administration.

context.concept_name: Distinguish capacity requirements from availability requirements

required_facts.statement: Redundant components and multiple locations can keep a workload available when a component fails.
Capacity must accommodate workload demand; adding or removing resources helps match capacity to changing demand.
For a component-failure constraint, evaluate independent redundant capacity rather than merely increasing the size of the same component.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: One requirement asks for more throughput during busy periods. Another asks for service to continue after a component fails. Both involve resources, but they ask different questions. Separate the amount of capacity from the independence of the capacity that remains after a failure.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Redundant components and multiple locations can keep a workload available when a component fails.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Capacity must accommodate workload demand; adding or removing resources helps match capacity to changing demand.

For a component-failure constraint, evaluate independent redundant capacity rather than merely increasing the size of the same component.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
Suppose a lab's demand requirement says it must handle 200 requests per second, while its failure requirement says it must keep serving after one component is lost. Increasing the size of a single component may address demand, but evaluating the failure requirement calls for independent redundant capacity. Write two conclusions: whether total capacity accommodates the supplied demand, and whether remaining independent components can meet the supplied service requirement after the loss. Adding or removing resources helps match changing demand; redundant components and multiple locations can support availability during a component failure. Keep the two requirements visible when comparing proposals, rather than accepting a larger component as the answer to both.

Now compare two illustrative proposals with equal total capacity: one larger component and two independent components. Under ordinary load they may both satisfy the supplied demand requirement. Under loss of the single larger component, its capacity is unavailable; with independent components, remaining capacity can be evaluated against the service requirement. Equal total capacity therefore does not settle the failure requirement. The record needs the surviving capacity question as well.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: More capacity in the same component is not the same as independent redundant capacity. For a component-failure constraint, evaluate the latter; for changing demand, evaluate whether the workload has enough capacity. One measure does not replace the other.

video_need.reason: A simple demand-versus-component-loss sketch suffices to distinguish capacity from independent redundant availability capacity.

practice_anchor.objective: Select one design change from supplied proposals for a lab facing either changing demand or loss of one component.
practice_anchor.success: For changing demand, select a resource adjustment that matches capacity to the supplied demand. For component loss, select independent redundant capacity whose surviving components meet the supplied service requirement, rather than merely enlarging the same component.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show one larger component beside two independent components with equal total capacity. Make ordinary-demand capacity and surviving capacity after one component is lost visible separately, alongside the supplied demand and service requirements.

teaching_notes: Defer specific scaling-policy and controlled-AZ-failure procedures.

required_facts.statement: Operational events need response processes with identified owners and escalation paths.
Assign event-response responsibility and document when and to whom unresolved issues are escalated.
Identify a team responsible for each resource and process so operators know whom to engage.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An operator has an unresolved event and needs to know who can take responsibility. A resource name alone is not enough for a handoff. The response process needs an accountable owner and a defined next responder when routine work cannot resolve the issue.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Operational events need response processes with identified owners and escalation paths.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Assign event-response responsibility and document when and to whom unresolved issues are escalated.

Identify a team responsible for each resource and process so operators know whom to engage.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content:
For a sandbox orders service, suppose the supplied ownership record names the application operations team for the service and a separate team for an associated process. Use those named responsibilities when preparing the event-response record. Document the condition that requires escalation and identify the recipient rather than writing only escalate if necessary. If the current operator reaches the stated unresolved-issue condition, the record should show whom to engage and why. This example does not invent a universal escalation time or chain; the responsible teams and conditions come from the established environment. The operational value is that a later responder can find responsibility for both the resource and the process without guessing.

Compare an entry that says operations handles issues with one that names the responsible team, the unresolved-issue condition and the next responder. Only the latter gives the current operator a definite handoff decision under that condition. If responsibility for a process differs from responsibility for its resources, record both rather than assuming a single resource owner covers every operational activity.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: An escalation path is more than a list of contacts. The response process must document when an unresolved issue moves on and to whom. Naming a team for each resource and process supplies the ownership context for that decision.

video_need.reason: Ownership and escalation are documentation requirements; a small owner/condition/recipient table suffices without a tool demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Complete an ownership and escalation record for the sandbox orders service using supplied established teams and escalation conditions. Select the service owner, associated-process owner, initial event responder, unresolved-issue escalation condition, and escalation recipient.
practice_anchor.success: The completed record matches the supplied responsibilities for both the service and its associated process, identifies who initially acts on an event, and specifies when and to whom an unresolved issue is escalated without inventing a new policy.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the sandbox orders service's resource and process responsibilities visible alongside the initial event responder, established unresolved-issue escalation condition, and next recipient.

teaching_notes: Use established owners and escalation conditions; do not author an organization-wide incident policy.

context.concept_name: Evaluate an IAM identity policy for a requested operation after external access-control preparation

required_facts.statement: An identity-based policy attaches to an identity and specifies permitted or denied actions on resources.
A statement uses Effect, Action and Resource, with optional Condition tests to scope when it applies.
For a request, compare action, resource and condition values with applicable statements; explicit deny overrides an allow, and absent an applicable allow the request is implicitly denied.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An operator requests a particular AWS action on a particular resource. A policy that looks permissive in general may not allow that request. Evaluate the request against the statement's actual action, resource and any conditions, using the access-control preparation already completed.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An identity-based policy attaches to an identity and specifies permitted or denied actions on resources.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
A statement uses Effect, Action and Resource, with optional Condition tests to scope when it applies.

For a request, compare action, resource and condition values with applicable statements; explicit deny overrides an allow, and absent an applicable allow the request is implicitly denied.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Consider supplied statements for an example object read. One Allow covers the requested action and the object's resource scope only when its Condition tests are satisfied. First compare the requested action with Action, then the target with Resource, then the request values with each applicable condition. If these checks do not find an applicable allow, the result is implicit deny. Now suppose an applicable Deny also covers the request: that explicit deny overrides the allow. Record which statement applies and which request values support the result rather than saying the policy allows reads in general. This example evaluates the identity-policy rules in this brief; it is not yet a full diagnosis of every policy type that can constrain AWS access.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: An Allow somewhere in a policy is not an allow for every request. Scope and conditions must match. An applicable explicit deny still wins over an allow, and no applicable allow leaves the request implicitly denied.

video_need.reason: A request-to-statement decision path makes scope, unsatisfied conditions, implicit deny and overriding explicit deny visible.

practice_anchor.objective: Evaluate supplied identity-policy statements against sandbox object-read requests with named actions, resource targets and condition values. Identify applicable statements and classify each request as allowed, explicitly denied or implicitly denied.
practice_anchor.success: Each request has the correct outcome supported by action, resource and condition comparisons. The results include an applicable allow, an unsatisfied condition leaving no applicable allow, a resource mismatch leaving no applicable allow, and an applicable explicit deny overriding an allow.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make request-to-statement matching visible: show each sandbox object-read request's action, resource and condition values alongside statement Effect, Action, Resource and Condition tests, with applicability and the resulting allow, explicit deny or implicit deny.

teaching_notes: Do not introduce session policies, boundaries or organization policies before their allowed contexts.

context.concept_name: Execute a GitHub Actions workflow with an appropriate runner

required_facts.statement: Workflow YAML files are stored in .github/workflows; on defines the triggering events.
jobs defines jobs, runs-on selects the runner, and steps lists actions invoked with uses or commands executed with run.
Inspect a workflow run’s job and step logs to verify which steps ran and which succeeded or failed.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A supplied delivery workflow needs a runner and an observable execution. Read the workflow as a description of when work begins, where each job runs and what each step does. Then use execution evidence to determine what actually happened.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Workflow YAML files are stored in .github/workflows; on defines the triggering events.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
jobs defines jobs, runs-on selects the runner, and steps lists actions invoked with uses or commands executed with run.

Inspect a workflow run’s job and step logs to verify which steps ran and which succeeded or failed.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: In an illustrative repository, locate the supplied YAML under .github/workflows. Read on to identify its triggering event, then locate the intended job under jobs. Its runs-on value selects that job's runner. In steps, distinguish an action referenced with uses from a supplied command executed with run. After the expected event, open that workflow run and inspect the job and step logs. Suppose the logs show two steps succeeded and the third failed: record those actual outcomes, not just the three steps declared in YAML. Keep the same run in view while following the evidence so that a log from another revision is not mistaken for this execution. The exercise uses supplied actions and commands, not independent application build logic.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Declared steps and completed steps are different evidence. The YAML describes the job and runner; the workflow run's logs establish which steps ran and whether they succeeded or failed. A runner selection alone is not proof of successful execution.

video_need.reason: Following one YAML job into runner selection and actual step logs benefits strongly from a workflow execution demonstration.

media.group_title: From workflow YAML to execution evidence

segments.label: Create a supplied workflow, trigger it, and inspect step logs
segments.summary: A Java/Gradle workflow template creates a YAML file under .github/workflows. Its event section specifies pushes to the master branch and pull requests targeting that branch. A job groups steps: uses invokes reusable actions for checking out the repository and preparing Java, while run executes supplied commands. The example requires an existing Java/Gradle application. Creating a pull request triggers the workflow, and opening its execution details reveals the completed steps. The logs distinguish executed commands from their output and show setup, checkout, Java preparation, a successful build, and automatic cleanup. These execution details establish what actually ran; the workflow declaration alone does not establish success.

bridge_note.before: Watch how the supplied template connects triggering events to a job, then follow that execution into step logs. Treat the application and commands as supplied inputs.
bridge_note.after: The clip explains jobs and uses/run steps but does not explain runs-on runner selection. The text supplies that missing link between the job and its runner.

practice_anchor.objective: Run a supplied build-and-test workflow in a prepared repository. Locate its YAML, identify the triggering event, and select the supplied runner option that matches the stated job requirements through runs-on. Use the prepared event control to start the workflow, then inspect its job and step logs.
practice_anchor.success: One workflow execution is associated with the expected event and runner selection. The learner records which supplied build-and-test steps ran and which succeeded or failed, using logs from that same execution rather than inferring outcomes from YAML.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the supplied workflow's path, on events, jobs, runs-on value, and uses/run steps visible alongside the corresponding execution's job and step logs, including executed-step statuses.

teaching_notes: Require external Git and pipeline-stage preparation; use supplied commands instead of introducing new shell syntax.

context.concept_name: Interpret DORA delivery and recovery evidence

coverage.learning_objective: Interpret DORA delivery and recovery evidence

required_facts.statement: Deployment frequency measures how often changes are deployed; change lead time measures the elapsed time for a committed change to reach production.
Change fail rate measures the proportion of deployments requiring intervention; failed deployment recovery time measures how long recovery from a failed deployment takes.
Compare throughput and instability measures together over time and within application context rather than using one measure to rank individuals.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A delivery report shows deployments are more frequent, but recovery evidence is also changing. Read throughput and instability together before proposing a conclusion about the delivery workflow.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: Deployment frequency measures how often changes are deployed; change lead time measures the elapsed time for a committed change to reach production.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Change fail rate measures the proportion of deployments requiring intervention; failed deployment recovery time measures how long recovery from a failed deployment takes.

Compare throughput and instability measures together over time and within application context rather than using one measure to rank individuals.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose one period has more deployments and shorter commit-to-production time, but a larger proportion of deployments need intervention. The first observations concern deployment frequency and change lead time; the latter concerns change fail rate. Add the failed-deployment recovery-time evidence to understand how long those failures take to recover from. Compare these measures over time for the same application context. Do not turn one improving measure into a ranking of individual operators.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: Frequent delivery alone does not describe stability. Keep failure proportion and failed-deployment recovery time beside throughput measures, and interpret the combined evidence within the application's context.

video_need.reason: The bounded metric interpretation needs only a throughput/stability comparison over time, not a workflow execution demonstration.

practice_anchor.objective: Interpret a supplied delivery dataset for the same application across two periods. Select the measures that support a throughput or stability concern and identify the supported concern.
practice_anchor.success: Correctly distinguishes deployment frequency and change lead time from change fail rate and failed deployment recovery time, selects evidence supporting the concern, and interprets it alongside the other measures without treating one metric as a complete performance score or ranking individuals.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show two comparable reporting periods for the same application, with deployment frequency, change lead time, change fail rate, and failed deployment recovery time side by side, making improving throughput and worsening stability visible together.

teaching_notes: Keep metric definitions and interpretation bounded; do not introduce unsupported performance benchmarks.

context.concept_name: Match operational events with EventBridge rules

required_facts.statement: An EventBridge event pattern describes event fields and values that an event must match.
Write a JSON object containing the fields to filter and arrays of acceptable values; fields omitted from the pattern are not required to match.
Test a pattern against both matching and nonmatching sample events with the EventBridge sandbox or TestEventPattern before using it in a rule.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: An event rule should select the intended operational events without selecting unrelated examples. Build the matching requirement from named event fields, then test the boundary with examples that should pass and examples that should not.

teaching_blocks.title: The operating model
teaching_blocks.content: An EventBridge event pattern describes event fields and values that an event must match.

teaching_blocks.title: How the check works
teaching_blocks.content:
Write a JSON object containing the fields to filter and arrays of acceptable values; fields omitted from the pattern are not required to match.

Test a pattern against both matching and nonmatching sample events with the EventBridge sandbox or TestEventPattern before using it in a rule.

teaching_blocks.title: Work through one sandbox case
teaching_blocks.content: Suppose the lab supplies events with source and detail-type fields. The intended pattern accepts source value lab.orders and detail-type value OrderReady. Represent each acceptable value in an array under its field in the JSON pattern. Test an event carrying those values, then change detail-type to OrderCancelled in a second sample and test again. Also test a sample that varies a field omitted from the pattern: omitted fields are not required to match. Compare each test result with the intended requirement before using the pattern in a rule. The names here are invented sample data; the event bus and real operational event fields must come from the supplied exercise. This stage teaches selection, not target execution permissions.

teaching_blocks.title: Do not confuse the evidence
teaching_blocks.content: A pattern is not a requirement that every field in the event be identical to a sample. Fields omitted from the pattern are not required to match. Positive and negative tests make the intended field-level selection explicit.

video_need.reason: Side-by-side pattern JSON and positive/negative events make field matching and omitted-field behavior visible.

practice_anchor.objective: Write one JSON event pattern accepting source lab.orders and detail-type OrderReady. Test supplied matching and nonmatching samples in the EventBridge sandbox before using the pattern in a rule.
practice_anchor.success: The pattern uses arrays of acceptable values under source and detail-type. A sample with lab.orders and OrderReady matches; a sample with lab.orders and OrderCancelled does not match. Both sandbox results agree with the intended selection.

live_code.required_skill: Express field-level event selection as a JSON pattern and verify it against positive and negative samples.
allowed_syntax: Double-quoted JSON field names and string values
Colons separating field names from values
JSON arrays of acceptable string values
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide an empty JSON pattern editor in the EventBridge sandbox and two complete sample events. Each includes id, account, source, time, region, resources, and detail-type. Use source lab.orders in both; use detail-type OrderReady in the first and OrderCancelled in the second. Keep all other supplied fields unchanged between the samples; vary detail-type as specified and give each sample a distinct event id; learners edit only the pattern.
live_code.observable_success: The completed pattern is {"source":["lab.orders"],"detail-type":["OrderReady"]}. Testing returns a match for the OrderReady sample and no match for the OrderCancelled sample.

visual_anchor.purpose: Place the JSON pattern beside matching and nonmatching sample events, marking each constrained field and its acceptable values. Include an additional supplied event field absent from the pattern and show that changing only that omitted field leaves the match result unchanged.

teaching_notes: Keep target authorization and delivery retries for their later concepts.
